index.answer: Subtract 1.5, which brings the mean squared error down to 4. The mean squared error is the mean of the squared error, so it equals the variance plus the squared mean: 6.25 = 2² + 1.5², and the mean error is +1.5 because the model over-forecasts. theory.title: How Often the Best Checkpoint Changes
overview: A training script measures the validation loss after each of 6 epochs and saves a checkpoint whenever the loss is the lowest seen so far, so the first epoch always saves. Suppose the model is not learning at all: the six losses are six different numbers in random order, and each of the $6! = 720$ orders is equally likely.

prompt.p: What is the expected number of checkpoints the script saves?

answer.p: Let $I_k$ be 1 if epoch $k$ saves, that is, if its loss is the smallest of the first $k$, and 0 otherwise. The number of saves is $I_1 + I_2 + \dots + I_6$.

The first $k$ losses are in random order, so each of them is equally likely to be the smallest of the $k$. The last one is the smallest with probability $1/k$, so $\mathbb{E}[I_k] = 1/k$. Linearity adds the six means:

Linearity holds whether or not the $I_k$ are independent. A model that learns nothing still saves a new best more than twice on average, so a few new bests in a log are no evidence that training works.

prompt.p: The script also flags an epoch whose loss is the highest seen so far, as a warning that training may be diverging. On average, how many of the six epochs set a new lowest loss, a new highest loss, or both?

answer.p: Let $J_k$ be 1 if epoch $k$ sets a new lowest or a new highest loss. Epoch 1 does both, so $J_1 = 1$. For $k \ge 2$, the last of the first $k$ losses is the smallest with probability $1/k$ and the largest with probability $1/k$, and it cannot be both, so $\mathbb{E}[J_k] = 2/k$. Linearity gives

Adding the expected number of new lows, 2.45, to the expected number of new highs, also 2.45, gives 4.9, which counts epoch 1 twice. The count is of epochs, and epoch 1 is one epoch that sets both records.

theory.title: Draws Until Every Class Has Appeared
overview: A data loader draws training examples one at a time, uniformly at random and with replacement, from a dataset with four equally common classes. Let $N$ be the number of draws until every class has appeared at least once.

prompt.p: What is $\mathbb{E}[N]$?

answer.p: Split the draws into four stages. Stage $j$ starts when $j - 1$ classes have appeared and ends at the draw that brings a new one. During stage $j$ each draw is new with probability $(5 - j)/4$, independently of the other draws, so the length of the stage is the number of trials up to and including the first success: Geometric with $p = 1, \tfrac34, \tfrac12, \tfrac14$.
$N$ is the sum of the four stage lengths, and linearity adds their means, $1/p$:
The last class alone takes 4 draws on average, nearly half the total, because by then three draws in four bring a class already seen.

prompt.p: What is the standard deviation of $N$?

answer.p: The four stage lengths are independent, since each stage only uses its own draws. So their variances add. A Geometric($p$) has variance $(1 - p)/p^2$:

The standard deviation is $\sqrt{130/9} \approx 3.80$ draws. The last stage gives 12 of the 14.44, about 83%. Adding the four standard deviations instead, $0 + 0.67 + 1.41 + 3.46 = 5.54$, would overstate the spread, since for independent pieces it is the variances that add.

theory.title: Send a Second Request Only When the First Is Slow
overview: A service answers a request in 1, 2 or 6 milliseconds, with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1, so its mean response time is 1.8 ms. A client sends each request to one copy of the service. If that copy has not answered after $d$ ms, that is, if its response time is more than $d$, the client sends the same request to a second copy and uses whichever answer arrives first. The two copies answer independently, each with this distribution, and $d$ is a whole number of milliseconds.

prompt.p: With $d = 2$, what is the client's expected wait in milliseconds?

answer.p: Call the response times $T_1$ and $T_2$. The second copy's answer arrives at time $2 + T_2$, so the wait is $W = \min(T_1,\ 2 + T_2)$. This also covers the requests that never send a second copy: when $T_1 \le 2$, the minimum is $T_1$ anyway.
The wait is at least $k$ exactly when both answers arrive at $k$ or later, and the two copies are independent, so
The tails of one copy are $P(T \ge 1) = 1$, $P(T \ge 2) = 0.4$, and $P(T \ge j) = 0.1$ for $j = 3, \dots, 6$. A tail at $j \le 1$ is 1. So for $k = 1, \dots, 6$:
The wait is never above 6, and the tail-sum formula gives $\mathbb{E}[W] = 1 + 0.4 + 0.1 + 0.04 + 0.01 + 0.01 = 1.56$ ms.

Squaring the tails, as if both copies started together, gives 1.2. That is the wait when every request goes to two copies at once, which doubles the load. With $d = 2$ only the requests still waiting at 2 ms, 10% of them, send a second copy, and they cut the mean from 1.8 ms to 1.56 ms.

prompt.p: The team wants an expected wait of at most 1.5 ms and as few second copies as possible. Which delay $d$ should it use, and what share of requests then send a second copy?

answer.p: A second copy goes out when $T_1 > d$: for every request when $d = 0$, for 40% when $d = 1$, and for 10% when $d$ is 2 to 5. A larger delay sends fewer copies and waits longer, so the answer is the largest $d$ that still meets 1.5 ms.

Part 1 gives 1.56 ms at $d = 2$, which misses. At $d = 1$ the same steps with $P(T_2 \ge k - 1)$ give the tails 1, 0.4, 0.04, 0.01, 0.01 and 0.01, so $\mathbb{E}[W] = 1.47$ ms, which meets it. The team should use $d = 1$, and 40% of requests send a second copy.

The trade-off is uneven. Sending both at once buys 0.6 ms for 100% more requests. A delay of 1 ms buys 0.33 ms for 40%, and a delay of 2 ms buys 0.24 ms for 10%. A delay of 2 ms sends a second copy only for the requests whose first answer will take 6 ms, which is why so few copies still help.

theory.title: The Ensemble Floor from Two Measurements
overview: A team measures the variance of an ensemble's averaged error at two sizes. With 2 models it is 3.0, and with 8 models it is 1.5. Every model has the same error variance, and every pair of models has the same correlation.

prompt.p: What value does the variance of the averaged error approach as the ensemble grows without limit?

answer.p: With $n$ models the variance is $\rho\sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\sigma^2/n$. Write it as $a + b/n$, with $a = \rho\sigma^2$ and $b = (1 - \rho)\sigma^2$. The two measurements give
Subtracting, $\tfrac38 b = 1.5$, so $b = 4$ and $a = 3 - 2 = 1$. As $n$ grows, $b/n$ goes to 0 and the variance approaches $a = 1$.

Scaling the 2-model result by $1/n$, as for independent errors, would put the 8-model variance at $3 \cdot 2/8 = 0.75$. The measured 1.5 is twice that, which already shows a shared part that averaging does not remove.

prompt.p: What is the correlation between the errors of two of the models?

answer.p: The floor $a = 1$ is $\rho\sigma^2$, not $\rho$ itself, so the correlation also needs each model's error variance. That is the case $n = 1$, an ensemble of one: $\sigma^2 = a + b = 1 + 4 = 5$. Then $\rho = a / \sigma^2 = 1/5 = 0.2$.

As a check, $5\,(0.2 + 0.8/2) = 3$ and $5\,(0.2 + 0.8/8) = 1.5$, the two measurements. A correlation of only 0.2 still leaves a floor of one fifth of a single model's variance, which no number of these models gets below.

The overall mean is $0.5 \cdot 60 + 0.25 \cdot 64 + 0.25 \cdot 72 = 64$, and the city means spread around it by
So the mean squared error is $40 - 24 = 16$. Measuring the city means from 0 instead of from 64, or leaving out the shares, gives a wrong spread.

theory.title: Three Correlations That Cannot All Be True
overview: A data report lists the correlations between three features: $\operatorname{corr}(A, B) = 0.9$, $\operatorname{corr}(B, C) = 0.9$ and $\operatorname{corr}(A, C) = -0.5$.

prompt.p: Show that no three random variables can have these correlations.

answer.p: Dividing each variable by its standard deviation leaves every correlation unchanged, so assume $A$, $B$ and $C$ have variance 1. Then each covariance equals the correlation, and the covariance matrix is
Any combination $\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}$ has variance $\mathbf{w}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{w}$, and a variance is never negative. Take $\mathbf{w} = (1, -1, 1)$, the combination $A - B + C$:

No random variables have a negative variance, so the three numbers cannot all be correct. The idea behind the choice of $\mathbf{w}$: $A$ and $C$ both track $B$ closely, so $A - B$ and $C - B$ are small, yet $A$ and $C$ are claimed to move apart.

prompt.p: Keep $\operatorname{corr}(A, B) = \operatorname{corr}(B, C) = 0.9$. What is the smallest value $\operatorname{corr}(A, C)$ can take?

answer.p: Call it $c$, keep unit variances, and try the combinations $A - tB + C$ for every number $t$:
This must be at least 0 for every $t$. The quadratic is smallest at $t = 1.8$, where it equals $3.24 - 6.48 + 2 + 2c = 2c - 1.24$. So $c \ge 0.62$.
The bound is reached. Take $B$ and $U$ independent with mean 0 and variance 1, and set
Each has variance $0.81 + 0.19 = 1$, each has covariance 0.9 with $B$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(A, C) = 0.81 - 0.19 = 0.62$. So the smallest possible value is $0.62$.

The same steps with both correlations equal to $r$ give $\operatorname{corr}(A, C) \ge 2r^2 - 1$. For $r$ above $1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.71$ the bound is positive: two features that both track a third that closely must be positively correlated with each other. Below it, they can be uncorrelated or even negatively correlated.

theory.title: A Test Set with Five Scans per Patient
overview: A model reads medical scans. Its test set has 300 scans, 5 from each of 60 patients, and on a random scan the model is right with probability 0.9. Two scans of the same patient look alike, so whether the model is right on one and whether it is right on the other have correlation 0.5. Scans of different patients are independent. The team reports the accuracy, the share of the 300 scans the model gets right.

prompt.p: What is the standard deviation of the reported accuracy?

answer.p: Let $J_i$ be 1 if the model is right on scan $i$. Each $J_i$ is Bernoulli with variance $0.9 \cdot 0.1 = 0.09$. The variance of $J_1 + \dots + J_{300}$ is the sum of all $300 \times 300$ covariances:

list: Each scan has 4 other scans of the same patient, so $300 \cdot 4 = 1{,}200$ cells hold $0.5 \cdot 0.09 = 0.045$, which adds $54$.
Every other cell pairs two patients and is 0.

answer.p: So the sum has variance 81, the accuracy (the sum divided by 300) has variance $81 / 300^2 = 0.0009$, and its standard deviation is $0.03$, or 3 percentage points.
Treating the 300 scans as independent would give $\sqrt{0.09/300} \approx 0.017$, too small by a factor of $\sqrt3$.

prompt.p: How many independent scans, each from a different patient, would give the accuracy the same standard deviation?

answer.p: With $N$ independent scans the accuracy has variance $0.09/N$. Setting $0.09/N = 0.0009$ gives $N = 100$. The 300 scans carry as much information about the accuracy as 100 independent ones. In general a group of $m$ scans with correlation $\rho$ multiplies the variance by $1 + (m - 1)\rho$, here $1 + 4 \cdot 0.5 = 3$, so the test set counts as $300/3$ scans.

prompt.p: The team keeps the same 60 patients and scans each of them more times. What standard deviation does the accuracy approach as the number of scans per patient grows? Can the team reach 0.015 this way?

answer.p: With $m$ scans of each of the 60 patients, the same count of covariance cells gives the accuracy the variance

This is the ensemble formula $\sigma^2\big(\rho + (1 - \rho)/m\big)$ for one patient's scans, divided by the 60 independent patients. As $m$ grows it falls toward $0.09 \cdot 0.5 / 60 = 0.00075$, a standard deviation of $\sqrt{0.00075} \approx 0.0274$. Ten scans per patient give 0.0287 and a thousand give 0.0274, never 0.015.

What the scans of one patient share does not average away, so only new patients bring the error down. With 5 scans each the accuracy has variance $0.054/k$ for $k$ patients, and a standard deviation of 0.015 takes $k = 0.054 / 0.015^2 = 240$ patients.
